The Story of Patrakesari

I pay homage to Acharya Patrakesari, who illuminated the path of right faith. His life story is told here, for it reveals how true vision is attained.

In this sacred land of Bharat, blessed by the five auspicious events of the Tirthankaras and bestowing happiness upon all living beings, there lay a country called Magadh — a place of great worldly splendour. Within it stood a beautiful city named Ahichhatra, whose beauty astonished all who beheld it.

Through the merit of its citizens, a king named Avanipal ruled there. He was a man of great virtue and a master of all the royal sciences. He governed his kingdom with wise policy. In his court served five hundred learned Brahmins, well-versed in the Vedas and their auxiliary texts, who assisted him ably in matters of state. Yet they carried one flaw — a great pride in their lineage, because of which they looked down upon everyone else. They performed their daily twilight rituals with scrupulous regularity. And there was one remarkable thing about them: before attending the royal court each day, they would first visit the sacred temple of Lord Parshvanath and pay their respects to the blessed Jina's image.

One day, having completed their evening rites, the Brahmins came to the Jina temple and there beheld a monk named Charitrbhushan reciting a hymn called the Devagam Stotra before the Lord. Patrakesari, the foremost among them, asked the monk, "Do you know the meaning of this hymn?" The monk replied honestly, "I do not know its meaning." Patrakesari then said, "Revered one, please read this hymn once more." The monk obliged, reading the Devagam slowly, pausing at the end of each phrase. All who listened felt great joy.

Now, Patrakesari possessed an extraordinary power of retention. He could memorize anything with just a single hearing. So too did he commit the entire Devagam to memory as it was read. He then began to contemplate its meaning deeply. Through the partial destruction and suppression of the karma that deludes one's vision, a certainty arose within him: what the Jina had taught about the nature of the soul and all other realities was the truth — and nothing else was.

Afterward, he returned home and continued to reflect upon the nature of reality. Days passed in this deep contemplation; even his nights were consumed by the same thought. He reasoned with himself: if these teachings are true, then the soul is distinct from the body, bound by karma, and capable of liberation through right faith, right knowledge, and right conduct. Worldly life, he saw, is impermanent and filled with suffering. The wise should therefore renounce attachment and pursue liberation.

With this conviction blazing in his heart, Patrakesari renounced his worldly life. He approached Acharya Charitrbhushan and took the vows of monkhood. As a monk, he observed the strictest conduct, practised severe austerities, and immersed himself in meditation. Through the fire of meditation he destroyed all destructive karmas and attained keval jnan — the infinite, omniscient knowledge that illuminates all worlds.

Having attained that supreme state, Patrakesari spent the rest of his life teaching the path of liberation to all who came to him. When his remaining lifespan drew to a close, he practised the ultimate austerity of sallekhana — the peaceful, voluntary renunciation of the body — and attained moksha, the eternal abode of bliss beyond all suffering.

Thus did Patrakesari, who began as a proud Brahmin scholar, become one of the greatest lights of the Jain tradition. His story reminds us that right faith can dawn upon anyone, at any time, when the inner readiness is there — and that even a single moment of true understanding can transform an entire life.
